scopeLede: The same job on paper can cost very differently in a lakeshore Victorian, a courtyard condo and a downtown tower. These are the things that change it, and most are settled at the walkthrough.

scopeRows.why: Permitted work in Evanston needs every contractor on the permit registered with the City, with a licence and a certificate of insurance naming the City.

Exterior work seen from the street, alley or sidewalk in a local historic district, such as moving a meter, a new service mast or exterior lighting, needs a Certificate of Appropriateness before a permit is issued.
Knob-and-tube, cloth-covered wire and fuse boxes still turn up in pre-1930 houses, and opening plaster changes the scope.
Older houses and two-flats often have 60- or 100-amp services. An EV charger, central air or a kitchen remodel can mean a 200-amp upgrade and a ComEd appointment.
Courtyard buildings and towers want a written proposal and a certificate of insurance before work in units or common areas.
Fishing wire through plaster and lath is slower than drywall and needs careful patching.
Many houses have a detached garage off the alley. A feed for an EV charger can mean trenching and new conduit.
Downtown and near Northwestern, parking is metered or permit-only, which changes how materials and crews get in.
Evanston usually requires a rough and a final inspection, and someone for the permit holder has to be on site for each.
Restaurants and occupied offices often need early, late or weekend work, so agree the hours before the job is scheduled.

hourlyAnswer: We quote by scope, not by the hour, because the hours on an Evanston job depend on the factors below. A fixture under a plaster ceiling in a 1915 courtyard condo and the same fixture in a new downtown tower aren't the same job. The written quote tells you the whole price before you agree to it.

reviews.text: As both a homeowner and long-time landlord, I am very skeptical about all contractors. I found Highlights Chicago Electrical Services on Yelp, and was even more skeptical regarding well over 200 five-star reviews. I needed a major electrical service upgrade done on a historic landmark apartment building I own so I had no choice but to do the research and select a contractor.  I know there are ways to get great reviews on Yelp. However, nine times out of ten, those people or "services" won't bother to write reviews in great detail, let alone many paragraphs in length. As I read through the reviews I realized they were legit.  I can now add mine to the list. This company has truly earned every five-star review it has received. I have NEVER had such a positive experience with an electrical contractor. Quite the opposite. I got 3 different estimates, and they weren't the lowest, and not the highest either. Boz came out to look at what needed to be done (which included undoing the disaster the previous electrician created) within a few hours of my call. He explained everything in detail, and the pro's and con's of what my options were.  They never asked for any payment upfront. The estimate was extraordinarily detailed. Shock number one. The team I was assigned, Kaplan and Jose, showed up ready to go at 7 am the next day! Shock number two. They worked their butts off until well after 6 pm! Shock number 3. They came back the next two days and did it again. Shock number 4.  This is a company that is proud of what they do. The end result looked like a work of art! The conduit was perfectly aligned, evenly spaced and so symmetrical I couldn't get over it. Every detail was addressed, and all done without cutting corners, dodging building codes, or overcharging. Old houses are not easy to work on and require a lot of patience and genuine expertise. They worked around all the challenges and knocked it out of the ballpark.  As long as they are in business, I will NEVER use anyone else. The few hundred dollars you might save going with the lowest cost option is nothing compared to the misery you will spare yourself by having this company do the work. If I could give them more stars I would. They are also really nice people to work with. When was the last time you thought that about a contractor?

faq.question: Are you registered to work in Evanston?
faq.answer: Yes. We're registered with the City of Evanston as an electrical contractor, registration 18LICL-0250, first issued in 2018. Evanston requires every contractor working under a permit to register with the City, and electricians register with a licence from a testing city such as Chicago, which issued ours, ECC96456.

faq.question: Do I need Preservation Commission approval for electrical work in an Evanston historic district?
faq.answer: Only for exterior work seen from the street, alley or sidewalk on a landmark or in a historic district, such as moving a meter, a new service mast or exterior lighting. Interior work isn't reviewed unless it changes the outside. The City's Property Quick Info map shows whether your address is in a district.

faq.question: Can you replace knob-and-tube or a fuse box in an older Evanston house?
faq.answer: Yes. We replace fuse boxes with breaker panels, upgrade 60- and 100-amp services, and rewire in stages so plaster patching stays small. The walkthrough is where we find out how much original wiring is left.

faq.question: Can you work in my Evanston condo building?
faq.answer: Yes. Associations in courtyard buildings and towers usually want a written proposal and a certificate of insurance first, and we pull the City of Evanston permit where the work needs one.

faq.question: Which Evanston ZIP codes do you cover?
faq.answer: All of Evanston: 60201, 60202 and 60203, including the blocks around Northwestern (60208), and the Chicago neighbourhoods across Howard St.

faq.question: Can you install an EV charger in a detached garage in Evanston?
faq.answer: Yes. We run a feed from the house panel to the garage, which can mean trenching and new conduit, and check first whether the service can carry the charger. If it can't, the service upgrade comes first.

scopeRows.why: Alta Vista Terrace, Hawthorne Place, Newport Avenue, Surf-Pine Grove and Terra Cotta Row are Chicago Landmark districts. The Commission on Chicago Landmarks reviews permits there, mainly for street-facing changes such as a service mast, a moved meter or facade lighting.
Many two-, three- and multi-flats still run on 100-amp services. A new service with a meter and panel for each unit needs a ComEd appointment as well as a City permit.
Older houses and flats can still have fuse boxes or cloth-covered wire, and opening a wall can show more original wiring than expected.
Fishing wire through plaster and lath in Lakeview's frame houses and vintage walk-ups is slower than drywall and needs careful patching.
Courtyard buildings, walk-up condos and towers usually want a written proposal and a certificate of insurance before work in units or common areas.
Lakefront towers book freight elevator time, set working hours and limit where boxes can go in concrete slabs.
Permit Parking Zone 383, from Belmont to Irving Park and Broadway to Ashland, is a tow zone from 5pm to 10pm on night games, and Addison can close around games.
A rear coach house or garage is fed from the front building. A new feed, subpanel or EV charger can mean new conduit along the gangway or across the yard.
Many stand-alone electrical jobs go through the City's Express Permit Program. Renovations, de-conversions and build-outs need plans and a standard review.
Signs are permitted separately from the electrical work, so a bar or shop refit may need two permits.
Bars and restaurants on Clark, Halsted and Broadway often need work before opening, so agree the hours before the job is scheduled.

faq.question: Do I need Landmarks approval for electrical work in a Lakeview landmark district?
faq.answer: Lakeview has five Chicago Landmark districts: Alta Vista Terrace, Hawthorne Place, Newport Avenue, Surf-Pine Grove and Terra Cotta Row on Oakdale Ave. The Commission on Chicago Landmarks reviews permits there as part of the normal building permit, mainly for changes to street-facing elevations, such as a service mast, a moved meter or facade lighting. No separate permit is needed, and our record includes a row house renovation on Alta Vista Terrace.

faq.question: Can you upgrade the service in my Lakeview two-flat or apartment building?
faq.answer: Yes. New services with a meter and panel for each unit are a large part of our Lakeview record, from four-unit buildings on N Bosworth Ave and W Eddy St to a 19-meter, 1,200-amp service on W Berteau Ave. We pull the City permit and coordinate the ComEd work.

faq.question: Do you work in Lake Shore Drive high-rises?

Our Lakeview record includes panel replacements and new kitchen circuits in units on the 3600 block of N Lake Shore Dr, lighting in a unit on the 3900 block and an alteration in a 44-storey condo building on the 2800 block. We work to the building's rules: a certificate of insurance, an elevator booking and set hours.

faq.question: Can you work in Wrigleyville on a game day?
faq.answer: Yes, but we plan for it. Permit Parking Zone 383, from Belmont to Irving Park and Broadway to Ashland, is a tow zone from 5pm to 10pm on night games, and Addison between Racine and Halsted can be closed around games, so we book Wrigleyville jobs around the Cubs schedule where we can.

faq.question: Can you power a coach house or detached garage?
faq.answer: Yes. A coach house or garage is fed from the front building, so we check the service first, then run the feed and add a subpanel if it's needed. Our Lakeview record includes coach house rehabs on N Racine Ave and W Roscoe St, a garage subpanel on W Cuyler Ave and an EV charger in a garage on N Lincoln Ave.

faq.answer: All of Lakeview: 60657 and 60613, from Diversey Pkwy up to Irving Park Rd and Montrose Ave, along with every other Chicago neighbourhood.

scopeLede: The same job on paper can cost very differently in a three-flat with a meter for every unit, an older house with a garage off the alley and an apartment building with 26 meters. These are the things that change it, and most are settled at the walkthrough.

scopeRows.why: Many older flats and houses here still have 100-amp services. An EV charger, central air or a kitchen remodel can mean a 200-amp service first.
In a two- or three-flat, an upgrade usually replaces a bank of meters and a panel for each unit, not one panel.
ComEd won't upgrade the service drop until the riser and weatherhead meet its rules, and its appointment sets the cut-over date.
Many lots have a garage off the alley. A charger or coach-house feed can mean trenching and underground conduit from the house.
Fuse boxes, cloth-covered wire and earlier owners' do-it-yourself work turn up in older houses and flats, and opening walls changes the scope.
These go under a full building permit with plans, not the Express Permit Program, and the electrical follows the architect's drawings and the builder's schedule.
A building with 15 to 26 meters needs a new main service, a meter bank and a panel per unit, scheduled with the owner around tenants.
Lincoln Ave shopfronts need tenant permits with plans, and work on a Chicago Landmark such as the Krause Music Store's facade is reviewed by the City's landmarks staff.
Parking near Lincoln Ave and the Brown Line stops is tight, which changes how materials and crews get in.
Shops and occupied buildings may need early or late work, and tenants in flats need notice before the power goes off. Agree the hours before the job is scheduled.
Service upgrades, new circuits and charger installs usually go through the City's Express Permit Program. 31 of our 52 Lincoln Square permits did.

hourlyAnswer: We quote by scope, not by the hour, because the hours on a Lincoln Square job depend on the factors below. Replacing a 100-amp service on a three-flat means three meters, three panels and a ComEd appointment, while adding one circuit in a house is a much smaller job. The written quote tells you the whole price before you agree to it.

scopeRows.why: Permit applications for buildings in the Logan Square Boulevards District go through the City's Historic Preservation Division, so plan exterior changes such as a moved meter, a new service mast or façade lighting around that review.
Many two- and three-flats still run on 60- or 100-amp services. An EV charger, central air or a new basement unit can mean a 200-amp service, a meter for each unit and a ComEd appointment.
A service upgrade on a two-, three- or four-flat replaces every unit's meter and panel, so the unit count sets much of the scope.
Buildings from the 1880s to the 1920s can still hide fuse boxes, cloth-covered wire and old DIY repairs behind the walls.
Fishing wire through plaster and lath in a greystone or two-flat is slower than drywall and needs careful patching.
A coach house can run from the front building or need its own service, risers and weatherhead, which ComEd can ask for before it upgrades a service.
Many houses have a garage off the alley. A feed for an EV charger can mean trenching and new conduit from the house panel.
A new house or small building is wired from the architect's drawings, with roof-deck, garage and unit-meter details settled before rough-in.
scopeRows.who: Your architect or builder, with us

scopeRows.why: On Milwaukee Ave a shop or restaurant often shares its building with the flats upstairs, which shapes how a fit-out is powered and when the work can happen.
Restaurants and occupied flats often need work planned around service hours or tenants, so agree the hours before the job is booked.
Service upgrades, EV circuits and unit work usually go through the City's Express Permit Program. New buildings and fit-outs need plans and a fuller review.

hourlyAnswer: We quote by scope, not by the hour, because the hours on a Logan Square job depend on the factors below. A new circuit in a Bucktown house built ten years ago and the same circuit behind the plaster of a boulevard greystone aren't the same job. The written quote tells you the whole price before you agree to it.

faq.question: Do I need landmark approval for electrical work on a Logan Square boulevard?
faq.answer: If your building is in the Logan Square Boulevards District, a Chicago Landmark district since 2005 along Logan, Kedzie, Palmer and Humboldt boulevards, the City's Historic Preservation Division reviews permit applications for work on it. The review checks that the work won't harm the building's historic features, so exterior changes such as moving a meter, a new service mast or façade lighting are the ones to plan around. Our own record includes a restaurant renovation in the district on W Armitage Ave.

faq.question: Can you upgrade the electrical service on my two-flat or three-flat?
faq.answer: Yes. It's one of our most common Logan Square jobs: replacing a 60- or 100-amp service with 200 amps and a new meter and panel for each unit. Our permits here include four-meter upgrades on N Avers Ave, N Monticello Ave and N Mozart St, and we arrange the ComEd side of the job.

faq.question: Can you wire a coach house or a basement conversion unit?
faq.answer: Yes, including a conversion unit in a two-flat on W Wrightwood Ave. The first question is whether the existing service can carry another unit or needs to be upgraded. The City's Additional Dwelling Unit rules decide whether the unit itself is allowed on your lot.

faq.question: Do you wire new houses and small buildings in Bucktown and Logan Square?
faq.answer: Yes. About half of our Logan Square permits are new construction: single-family houses and two- to four-unit masonry buildings, many with rooftop decks and detached garages. We work from the architect's drawings, pull the electrical permit and see it through inspection.

faq.question: Can you put an EV charger in my garage off the alley?
faq.answer: Usually, yes. Most chargers need one new circuit. If the garage is detached, the feed runs from the house panel, which can mean trenching, and if the service can't carry the charger the upgrade comes first. Our Logan Square record includes charger circuits on N Milwaukee Ave, N Drake Ave and N Spaulding Ave.

faq.question: Which Logan Square ZIP codes do you cover?
faq.answer: All of them. Most of Logan Square is 60647, and its edges fall in 60614, 60618, 60622 and 60639. We cover every other Chicago neighbourhood too.

scopeRows.factor: Building approval and certificate of insurance
scopeRows.why: Most managed buildings won't schedule work until they have both, and some name specific insurance limits.
Booked time windows decide when materials and crews get in, and how long a day on site really is.
Most West Loop streets have little parking near the door, so carrying tools and materials in takes time.
Wire can be fished through wood framing, has to run in conduit across concrete, or needs approved core drilling through a slab.
In a loft, conduit is part of the look. It's planned so it reads as intentional, which takes longer than hidden wiring.
Heavy chandeliers on 14-foot-plus ceilings need the right support, the right box and sometimes a lift.
Restaurants and occupied offices often need early, late or weekend work, so agree the hours before the job is scheduled.
In high-rises, fire alarm and life-safety tie-ins go through the building's own contractor.
Many unit jobs go through the City's Express Permit Program. Build-outs need plans and a standard review.
Boards often want a written proposal before they approve work in common areas or shared garages.
Whose meter the charger runs from, the building's spare capacity, and submetering decide the design.

hourlyAnswer: We quote by scope, not by the hour, because the hours on a West Loop job depend on the factors below. A fixture swap in a walk-up and the same fixture on a 16-foot loft ceiling aren't the same job. The written quote tells you the whole price before you agree to it.

faq.question: Do you work in West Loop high-rise buildings?
faq.answer: Yes. We work to the building's rules: a certificate of insurance before scheduling, booked freight elevator time, approved working hours and the building engineer's sign-off where it's needed. Reviewers describe our crews handling high-rise parking, elevators and building rules without fuss.

faq.question: Can you install an EV charger in my condo building's garage?
faq.answer: Usually, yes. The design depends on whose electrical service the charger runs from, the building's spare capacity, whether the association wants a submeter, and its approval process. We provide the certificate of insurance and a proposal the association can review.

faq.question: Do I need a permit for electrical work in my West Loop condo?
faq.answer: Most electrical work in Chicago needs a permit, and many unit jobs go through the City's Express Permit Program. Our own West Loop record includes permitted lighting work in condo units. We tell you at the walkthrough whether your job needs one, and we pull and close it.

faq.question: Do you work on restaurants on Randolph Street and in Greektown?
faq.answer: Yes: kitchen equipment circuits, service upgrades, lighting, emergency and exit lighting, and signage, scheduled around service. Our West Loop record includes a restaurant build-out on S Halsted.

faq.question: Which West Loop ZIP codes do you cover?
faq.answer: All of them: 60607, 60661 and the part of 60606 west of the river, along with every other Chicago neighbourhood.

scopeRows.why: In the Wicker Park District and the Milwaukee Avenue District, the Commission on Chicago Landmarks reviews alterations to buildings, so exterior electrical work such as a service mast, a meter move, exterior lighting or a sign can need its sign-off before the permit is issued.
Houses and flats built between the 1870s and the 1920s can still hide knob-and-tube, cloth-covered cable or a fuse box behind later remodels.
Two- and three-flats often still share a 100-amp service. Our upgrades on N Oakley Blvd moved buildings to 200 amps with three or four new meters and panels.
Fishing wire through plaster is slower than drywall, and openings are kept small so patching stays small.
Turning a three-flat back into one house, or digging out a basement, means a new service and every circuit redesigned from the architect's plans.
scopeRows.who: You and us, with your architect

scopeRows.why: Power for a garage or an EV charger means a feed from the house, sometimes underground, sized for what you'll run.
A new business sign needs its own sign permit, separate from the electrical permit.
In flats that are now condos, the association approves work in the basement, on the meters and in common areas, usually from a written proposal.
Parking near the door is scarce on Milwaukee, Division and North Ave, so on many jobs materials come in from the alley.
Stand-alone electrical jobs usually go through the City's Express Permit Program. New buildings, renovations and build-outs need plans and a full permit.
Bars, restaurants, shops and daycares often need work before opening or after closing, so agree the hours before the job is scheduled.

hourlyAnswer: We quote by scope, not by the hour, because the hours on a Wicker Park job depend on the factors below. A new circuit in a gutted three-flat on Campbell and the same circuit fished through the plaster of a Victorian on Hoyne aren't the same job. The written quote tells you the whole price before you agree to it.

faq.question: Does the Wicker Park landmark district change electrical work?
faq.answer: It can, if the work changes the outside. The Wicker Park District, around the park from Potomac Ave to Caton St, and the Milwaukee Avenue District are City landmark districts, and the Commission on Chicago Landmarks reviews alterations there as part of the permit. A new service mast, a moved meter, exterior lighting or a sign can need its sign-off, and we check at the walkthrough whether yours does.

faq.question: Can you upgrade the service in my Wicker Park two- or three-flat?
faq.answer: Yes. Our Wicker Park record includes two buildings on N Oakley Blvd moved from 100-amp to 200-amp services, with three and four new meters and panels. We pull the permit, usually through the City's Express Permit Program, and work with ComEd on the service change.

faq.question: Do you wire de-conversions and gut rehabs?
faq.answer: Yes. On the 1200 block of N Hoyne we did the electrical for a three-unit building turned back into one house with a two-storey addition, and on the 1300 block of N Wolcott an interior remodel of a four-unit building with a basement dig-down. These run under a permit with plans, and we work from your architect's drawings.

faq.question: Do you do the electrical for new houses and three-flats in Wicker Park?
faq.answer: Yes. Half our Wicker Park permits, 17 of 34, are new construction: houses with detached garages on N Campbell, N Artesian, N Wood and N Marion Ct, buildings of two to six units on N Paulina, N Claremont, N Artesian, N Campbell, N Wood and N Honore, and a four-storey mixed-use building on W North Ave.

faq.question: Can you work on a storefront on Milwaukee Ave, Division St or North Ave?
faq.answer: Yes: build-outs, lighting, signs and service work, scheduled around your hours. Our record includes daycare build-outs on W Division and W North Ave, and a tenant space and its sign on N Milwaukee. A new sign needs its own sign permit, and on Milwaukee Ave it can also need landmark review.

faq.question: Which Wicker Park ZIP codes do you cover?
faq.answer: Both: 60622, which covers most of Wicker Park, and 60647, which covers the blocks north of North Ave and west of Damen. We cover every other Chicago neighbourhood too.
